To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
older adults are more affected by the visual component of speech when the auditory input is degraded and the semantic context of speech is unknown.
older adults benefit more from audio–visual than unisensory speech when the speech is semantically meaningless.

(i) older adults have a higher cost for audio–visual speech when the visual component is degraded, compared to audio–only speech, (ii) this cost is higher when the speech is semantically meaningless and (iii) this effect is not present in younger adults.

the effects of aging on audio–visual speech perception.

audio–visual speech perception in older people is affected by both bottom-up sensory and top-down semantic processing.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

older adults are less likely to integrate multisensory information for speech if the visual component is blurred, but they benefit from multisensory information when the semantic content is predictable.

older adults benefit from audio–visual integration when the semantic content is predictable, but this benefit is reduced when the visual information is unreliable and/or when the semantic content cannot be anticipated.
the semantic content of speech is a crucial determinant for audio–visual integration in older adults.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the integration of multisensory inputs is not automatic and is dependent on the reliability of the information provided by the different modalities.
older adults may benefit from the use of multisensory speech perception, but only when the visual component of the speech is clear.
